etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English soken, from Old English socian (“to soak, steep”, literally “to cause to suck (up)”), from Proto-Germanic *sukōną (“to soak”), causative of Proto-Germanic *sūkaną (“to suck”). Cognate with Middle Dutch soken (“to cause to suck”). More at suck.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be saturated with liquid by being immersed in it.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 24:7:
quote.text: Their land shall be soaked with blood.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To immerse in liquid to the point of saturation or thorough permeation.
(intransitive) To penetrate or permeate by saturation.

quote.citation: 1815 February 24, [Walter Scott], Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […]  James Ballantyne and Co. for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, […]; and Archibald Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The rivulet beneath  […] soaked its way obscurely through wreaths of snow.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To allow (especially a liquid) to be absorbed; to take in, receive. (usually + up)

quote.citation: 1927, F. E. Penny, chapter 4, in Pulling the Strings:
quote.text: The case was that of a murder. It had an element of mystery about it, however, which was puzzling the authorities. A turban and loincloth soaked in blood had been found; also a staff.

definitions.definition: (slang, figurative, transitive) To overcharge or swindle out of a large amount of money.

quote.text: It's a blackmail ring, and the district attorneys get a share of the loot.  […]  Well, they got him in the same kind of jam, and soaked him to the tune of three hundred and eighty-six thousand.

quote.citation: 2015, P. J. O'Rourke, Thrown Under the Omnibus: A Reader:
quote.text: Sure, if we own an aerospace contracting company, a five-thousand-acre sugar-beet farm, or a savings and loan with the president's son on the board of directors, we can soak Uncle Sucker for millions.

definitions.definition: (slang, dated) To drink intemperately or gluttonously.
(metallurgy, transitive) To heat (a metal) before shaping it.
(ceramics, transitive) To hold a kiln at a particular temperature for a given period of time.

quote.citation: 1624, Henry Wotton, The Elements of Architecture, […], London:  […]  Iohn Bill, →OCLC:
quote.text: That they will want a certaine sucking and soaking

definitions.definition: (slang, chiefly Mormonism) To engage in penetrative sex without hip thrusting.[1]

quote.citation: 2020 February 25, Christopher de Bellaigue, “The end of farming?”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: wildlife tourism has turned Knepp into a successful business that employs more people than it did when it was a farm. Springtime overnighters snuggling down in a luxury treehouse after a soak in the open-air, wood-fired Swedish Hikki bathtub may hear nightingales serenading their consorts

definitions.definition: (Australia) A low-lying depression that fills with water after rain.

quote.citation: 1985, Peter Carey, Illywhacker, Faber & Faber, published 2003, page 38:
quote.text: I set off early to walk along the Melbourne Road where, one of the punters had told me, there was a soak with plenty of frogs in it.

quote.citation: 1996, Doris Pinkington, Follow the Rabbit-Proof Fence, in Heiss & Minter, Macquarie PEN Anthology of Aboriginal Literature, Allen & Unwin 2008, p. 170:
quote.text: Molly and Daisy finished their breakfast and decided to take all their dirty clothes and wash them in the soak further down the river.
